## AI-Designed Drug Shows Positive Phase II Results, Marking a First for the Field

Insilico Medicine published Phase IIa data in Nature Medicine in June 2025 for rentosertib, a drug candidate for idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis that was both discovered and designed by AI. The results were striking: patients on the highest dose showed a mean lung function improvement of 98.4 milliliters over twelve weeks, compared with a 20.3-milliliter decline in the placebo group.

IPF is a fatal lung disease with a median survival of just three to four years. Existing treatments only slow the scarring process. Rentosertib is the first drug with both an AI-discovered target and an AI-designed molecule to show positive mid-stage clinical results. A Phase III trial is now underway.

### How AI Compressed the Timeline

Traditional drug development takes 10 to 15 years and costs over $1 billion per approved drug, with a clinical success rate below 10 percent. Insilico reached preclinical candidate nomination for rentosertib in roughly 18 months for about $2.6 million, compared with the 4.5 to 6 years and hundreds of millions typically spent on that stage.

The company's AI platform, Pharma.AI, identified TNIK as a novel drug target and then designed a molecule to inhibit it. The system analyzed protein structures, genomic data, and published research to propose candidates that human chemists then refined. Insilico did not replace its scientists; it gave them tools that narrowed the search space from millions of potential molecules to a shortlist of promising candidates.

### The Pipeline Is Growing

Rentosertib is not an isolated case. As of mid-2026, over 173 AI-discovered drug programs are in clinical development, up from 67 in 2023 and just 3 in 2016, according to industry pipeline tracking. Major pharmaceutical companies have taken notice.

Novo Nordisk partnered with AWS in 2025 to bring agentic AI into drug discovery. Eli Lilly announced a co-innovation lab with NVIDIA in January 2026. Stanford researchers demonstrated a virtual laboratory where AI agents independently propose, design, and verify experiments with minimal human input. MIT used generative AI to design novel antibiotics against drug-resistant bacteria, screening over 36 million compounds computationally.

### The Hard Part Is Still Ahead

Compressing the discovery phase does not compress clinical trials. Rentosertib still needs to pass Phase III, which typically takes three to five years and enrolls hundreds or thousands of patients. No AI-discovered drug has received FDA approval yet. The 173 programs in clinical development will face the same attrition rates as any other drug candidate, with roughly 90 percent failing.

Skeptics also point out that AI's biggest wins so far have been in target identification and molecular design, the earliest and cheapest stages of drug development. The expensive, high-failure clinical phases remain stubbornly human. AI can optimize trial design and patient recruitment, as McKinsey has noted, but it cannot shortcut the years of safety and efficacy data required for approval.

Still, the rentosertib results changed the conversation. For the first time, AI has produced a drug candidate that not only works in a petri dish but improves patient outcomes in a controlled trial. That is no small thing.

## A Scale No One Has Demonstrated

The Google Kubernetes Engine team revealed that it successfully built and operated a Kubernetes cluster with 130,000 nodes—the largest publicly disclosed cluster to date. The achievement required re-architecting core components of Kubernetes itself, most notably replacing etcd, the conventional distributed key-value store, with a custom storage layer built on Google Cloud Spanner.

The milestone matters because Kubernetes clusters at major cloud providers typically top out in the tens of thousands of nodes. At that scale, etcd becomes a bottleneck due to write amplification, watch fan-out, and leader election overhead. API servers struggle under the constant stream of node heartbeats and pod status updates that a cluster of this size generates every second.

Google's team described the engineering effort in detail at a cloud infrastructure event. The project was driven by the needs of AI workloads, which often require hundreds or thousands of GPUs across a single cluster. Managing those resources across multiple smaller clusters introduces operational complexity, networking overhead, and resource fragmentation.

## How They Did It

Google's engineering team offloaded cluster state into Spanner, gaining horizontal scalability, global consistency, and automatic sharding of API objects including nodes, pods, and resource leases. The move eliminated the consensus bottleneck that caps most Kubernetes clusters. Spanner's ability to scale writes across multiple nodes removed the single-leader constraint that makes etcd vulnerable to write saturation at high node counts.

API servers were also refactored to batch and compress watch traffic, preventing control-plane saturation from the constant chatter of 130,000 nodes reporting status. In a standard Kubernetes cluster, each node sends regular heartbeats and pod status updates, and every API server watches those updates. At 130,000 nodes, the raw volume of watch events can overwhelm the control plane without batching and compression.

For node provisioning, the team introduced parallelized, automated node pool management that avoids thundering-herd problems when tens of thousands of nodes join simultaneously. Scheduling logic was optimized to handle the volume of pending pods that a cluster this size generates. The scheduler needed to make placement decisions across a vastly larger resource pool while maintaining acceptable latency for pod startup.

## Why It Matters Beyond Google

Most enterprises will never operate a cluster at 130,000 nodes. But the engineering work feeds back into the Kubernetes ecosystem. The bottlenecks Google identified—and the patterns for solving them—inform how managed Kubernetes services from AWS, Azure, and others scale their control planes. The project also validates approaches that other large-scale operators can adapt, even at smaller scales.

The demonstration validates Kubernetes as a platform for AI-era workloads that demand massive GPU and CPU clusters. As model training jobs require thousands of accelerators, the ability to manage them under a single control plane reduces operational complexity and improves resource utilization. Multi-cluster approaches like cluster federation have existed for years, but they introduce their own complexity around networking, identity, and workload placement.

Google has not disclosed whether the 130,000-node configuration will become a generally available GKE feature. For now, it stands as a proof of concept that pushes the boundary of what cloud-native infrastructure can handle and gives the Kubernetes community a target for future scalability work.

## The Data Transfer Problem

Serverless computing has matured beyond its initial use case as a platform for simple event-driven functions. In experiments across five real FaaS workflow applications, FineFlow reduced data transfer latency by up to 74.6% and an average of 63.8%, while cutting end-to-end execution time by 19.6%. For workflows with fine-grained data dependencies, the improvements were even more pronounced compared with existing data-locality optimizations.

The system works by constructing a directed acyclic graph of function dependencies, identifying the critical path through the workflow, and co-locating functions that exchange large volumes of data. This reduces the amount of data that must traverse the network and mitigates the impact of bandwidth fluctuations on execution consistency.

Academic research published in 2025 surveyed optimization techniques including remote container forking via RDMA (MITOSIS), language-aware function scheduling to group same-runtime functions (XFaaS), snapshot-based startup with memory block reuse across the cluster (Medes), and predictive container pre-warming based on execution time distributions (ORION). Each approach trades off memory overhead, prediction accuracy, and startup speed differently.

Cloud providers have also expanded their serverless portfolios. Tencent Cloud's CloudBase offers a full-stack serverless environment with cloud functions, databases, static hosting, and storage, with CI/CD integration through its CLI. AWS Lambda and Azure Functions continue to add language support and configuration options for provisioned concurrency, which keeps functions warm to eliminate cold starts for latency-sensitive workloads.

For developers, the message is that serverless is no longer just about individual functions. The tooling, standards, and research are now focused on making multi-function workflows performant, observable, and cost-effective at enterprise scale. The remaining challenge is educating engineering teams accustomed to serverful architectures on how to design applications that take full advantage of the model—stateless functions, event-driven triggers, and pay-per-execution pricing rather than always-on servers.

## Resizing Without Restarting

Kubernetes v1.34, codenamed "Of Wind & Will," brings in-place pod vertical scaling closer to stable after the feature graduated to beta in v1.33. For years, changing CPU and memory resources allocated to a running container required deleting and recreating the entire pod—a disruptive operation for stateful services, batch jobs, and latency-sensitive workloads. In-place pod resize makes those fields mutable, allowing resource adjustments without pod restarts.

The feature works by distinguishing between desired resources, specified in the pod specification, and actual resources, reflected in the container status. A resize subresource triggers the update, and the kubelet applies it without restarting the container where possible. The capability is foundational for vertical autoscaling, allowing clusters to right-size workloads dynamically based on actual usage rather than initial estimates that often over-provision resources to accommodate peak loads.

For platform teams, the impact is practical. A database pod that experiences a temporary traffic spike can be scaled up without dropping connections. A batch job that needs more memory midway through execution can be resized without losing progress. Over time, the feature should reduce the waste that comes from setting static resource requests based on worst-case scenarios.

## What Else Is New

The release includes dozens of enhancements across special interest groups. Configurable horizontal pod autoscaler tolerance, now in beta, lets users override the default scaling threshold on a per-HPA basis. That gives operators finer control over when workloads scale up or down, reducing churn from aggressive autoscaling that reacts to transient traffic spikes rather than sustained load changes.

SIG Apps promoted maxUnavailable for StatefulSets to beta, allowing operators to control how many pods can be unavailable during updates. The Job API's managed-by mechanism went stable, enabling third-party controllers to manage Job resources—a capability that benefits batch processing and AI training frameworks that need custom job scheduling beyond the built-in controller. Mutable container resources for suspended Jobs were also introduced, letting operators adjust CPU, memory, and GPU requests before a job resumes.

On the networking side, SIG Network deprecated the IPVS kube-proxy mode, marking the first step toward eventual removal. IPVS was introduced to handle larger cluster sizes than iptables could manage, but nftables and eBPF-based kube-proxy modes have since emerged as more maintainable alternatives with better performance characteristics. Cluster administrators running IPVS mode should plan migration to nftables or another supported mode.

SIG Auth advanced pod certificates to beta, enabling workloads to request X.509 certificates directly from the API server. The ensure-secret-pulled-images feature also went beta and is enabled by default, with kubelet tracking private image pulls to prevent unauthorized pods from using images pulled with another pod's credentials.

## The Road Ahead

Kubernetes follows a roughly four-month release cadence. The next version, v1.35, is expected to graduate in-place pod resize to stable, along with advancements in pod certificates and other beta features. The community continues to balance new feature development with cleanup, deprecating legacy APIs and removing alpha features that never gained traction. For platform teams, v1.34 is a practical upgrade rather than a dramatic shift. The in-place resize beta is worth testing for anyone running stateful workloads that currently over-provision resources.

## Encryption is the last step, not the first

On February 21, 2024, a Black Basta affiliate encrypted systems at UnitedHealth Group's Change Healthcare unit. The attack interrupted prescription claims for about 190 million Americans, delayed payments to physicians, and led UnitedHealth to pay a $22 million ransom. Its 2024 SEC filing put direct costs at $872 million.

For years, companies answered ransomware with backups. Backups still matter, but the Change Healthcare case showed why they are no longer enough. The attacker moved through remote access and identity systems before touching files. By the time ransom notes appeared, the incident was already a business outage.

## Identity alerts now lead the response

Mandiant's M-Trends 2025 report put median dwell time at nine days. That sounds fast, but ransomware operators do not need nine days once they reach a privileged account. A compromised help-desk account, a forgotten service principal, or a domain controller can give them the access needed to deploy encryption at scale.

CrowdStrike, Microsoft Defender, and SentinelOne now compete on identity detections as much as malware signatures. They look for impossible travel, new MFA methods added at odd hours, mass changes to Group Policy, and unusual use of backup tools. Defenders should also enforce just-in-time administration and remove local administrator rights from standard laptops.

## Patch the path, not just the payload

Many 2025 ransomware incidents still start with known issues: exposed RDP, unpatched VPN appliances, and vulnerable drivers. CISA's Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog gives security teams a practical triage list. If a CVE appears there, the normal 90-day patch cycle is too slow.

Bring-your-own-vulnerable-driver attacks remain a favorite way to disable EDR. Microsoft's vulnerable driver blocklist, Windows Smart App Control, and vendor tamper protection should be enabled on endpoints that support them. Domain controllers, hypervisors, and backup servers need separate hardening because those systems become high-value targets immediately.

## Test recovery like a product launch

Immutable storage protects backup data, but a restore is useless if no one has practiced it. Teams should time the recovery of Active Directory, identity providers, cloud tenants, and key applications. They should also document manual claims processing, payment rerouting, and communication plans for hospitals, pharmacies, or customers.

The economics are changing for attackers too. In the first quarter of 2025, multiple ransomware groups collapsed, rebranded, or lost negotiation sites, but the remaining operators shifted to faster extortion, data leaks, and help-desk impersonation. They know encrypted files trigger a visible crisis, while stolen credentials and exfiltrated data can be monetized with less noise. That is why detection engineers should build alerts around the setup phase: unusual access to hypervisors, changes to backup repositories, new scheduled tasks on domain controllers, and use of remote management software outside approved change windows. The goal is not to block every known binary. It is to interrupt the chain before the first production volume is encrypted.

Change Healthcare changed the ransomware conversation because the damage was visible outside IT. The companies that recover fastest in 2025 will not simply have clean backups. They will have limited privilege, continuous identity monitoring, and rehearsed business processes that keep running while systems come back.

## The network perimeter stopped matching work

OMB memorandum M-22-09 required federal agencies to reach baseline zero-trust goals by the end of fiscal 2024. In May 2025, agency inspectors general and CISA reviews still point to the same unfinished work: phishing-resistant authentication, asset visibility, and consistent access policies across cloud and on-premises systems.

The firewall-centric model assumed users and devices were already inside a trusted office network. That assumption broke when work moved to SaaS, personal devices, contractors, and APIs. Microsoft's 2024 Digital Defense Report tracked more than 600 million identity attacks per month. A stolen password is often worth more than a compromised port.

## Policy follows the user and device

Modern zero-trust programs do not start by replacing every network device. They start with policy decisions in Okta, Microsoft Entra ID, Zscaler, Palo Alto Prisma Access, or comparable platforms. A user accessing Salesforce from a managed laptop on a corporate network may get full access. The same user on an unmanaged device in a sanctioned country may get only a browser session with download restrictions.

That requires device signals. Intune, Jamf, CrowdStrike Falcon, and Microsoft Defender can tell the policy engine whether a device is encrypted, patched, running EDR, and subject to tampering. Without those signals, conditional access becomes a blunt rule based only on user and location.

## The first measurable win is privilege reduction

Zero trust can become a vague architecture exercise. The practical first metric is standing privilege. Companies should count global admins, root accounts, service accounts with broad cloud rights, and shared production logins. Then they should cut that number and replace permanent access with just-in-time approval.

This is where CyberArk, BeyondTrust, Delinea, and Okta Privileged Access compete. Their job is not only to vault passwords. It is to create an audit trail for each privileged action, enforce approval workflows, and rotate credentials automatically.

Many organizations discover that legacy systems block the cleanest architecture. Industrial control systems, old network appliances, and point-of-sale devices may not support device certificates or modern MFA. Those exceptions need documented compensating controls: jump hosts, network isolation, session recording, and time-limited access. They should not become permanent holes. Network teams also need logs from every access decision. A denied sign-in, a downgraded session, or an approved elevation is useful data for auditors and incident responders. If the access platform cannot export those events or tie them to a change ticket, it becomes a blind spot. Mature projects treat policy as code, test it like software, and review exceptions every quarter.

## Metrics that survive a board review

A useful zero-trust scorecard tracks phishing-resistant MFA coverage, managed-device percentage, privileged accounts with time-bound access, and blocked legacy authentication. It should also show how often access decisions were downgraded, revoked, or challenged.

Zero trust will never be finished. New contractors, acquisitions, AI assistants, and developer tools keep expanding the access surface. But the companies making progress in 2025 are not buying a single product called zero trust. They are forcing every access request to prove who is asking, what device they are using, and why the request should be allowed.

## One-time codes are not enough

In 2024, Microsoft Threat Intelligence described Storm-1167, a financially motivated group that sent millions of phishing messages, used adversary-in-the-middle proxies, and then called victims while posing as help-desk staff. The campaign showed a basic but expensive truth: a six-digit code entered on a fake login page can be relayed to the real login page in real time.

AiTM kits such as EvilProxy, Tycoon, and MrAnon do not try to crack MFA. They sit between the victim and Microsoft 365, Okta, or another identity provider. After the user logs in, the kit collects the session cookie. The attacker then replays that cookie from another device and often skips the second factor entirely.

## Passkeys break the relay

The most direct defense is phishing-resistant authentication. FIDO2 passkeys are device-bound and origin-bound. A passkey issued for login.microsoftonline.com will not authenticate on a proxy domain that pretends to be Microsoft. That property matters more than the fact that users no longer type a password.

Google, Microsoft, Apple, eBay, and PayPal have all expanded passkey support. Enterprises should prioritize high-risk roles first: executives, finance, IT administrators, and HR. Hardware security keys remain a strong option for users who need a clear separation between work and personal devices.

## Logs reveal the session heist

Conditional access does not stop every phishing message, but it makes replay harder. Policies should require managed or compliant devices for sensitive apps, block legacy authentication, and enforce location or risk checks. Microsoft Entra ID sign-in logs show token protection status, legacy clients, impossible travel, and suspicious MFA behavior. Okta System Logs show new devices, suspicious credential use, and MFA fatigue patterns.

Security teams should also tune their SIEM to alert on new OAuth consent grants, inbox-forwarding rules created after a phishing click, and access from Tor or known VPN exit nodes. Proofpoint, Abnormal, Microsoft Defender for Office 365, and Avanan can reduce message volume, but users still need a one-click report button.

Help-desk teams need their own rulebook. Attackers increasingly phone employees, claim they see a suspicious sign-in, and pressure them to read a code or approve a prompt. The solution is not another training video alone. It is a defined identity-verification process and a ban on MFA approvals requested through inbound calls. Finance workflows should require out-of-band confirmation through known numbers, in-person approvals, or payment portals rather than email replies. Phishing simulations should also measure reporting speed, not click rates. A user who clicks and reports within two minutes is less dangerous than one who ignores the message and never tells security. That reporting culture creates the early warning that stops a stolen cookie from becoming a breached tenant.

## Training should change behavior, not check a box

Annual training is easy to game. Better programs run monthly simulations, reward immediate reporting, and follow clicks within hours. Finance teams should see BEC scenarios. IT teams should see fake password resets. Executives should see messages tailored to their public schedules.

MFA still helps, but SMS codes and mobile push are no longer sufficient against serious phishing. The effective stack in 2025 is simple: phishing-resistant credentials, risk-based access, rapid user reporting, and detections that start the moment a suspicious session token appears.

## The breach was not a cloud zero-day

In 2024, intrusions tied to UNC5537 exposed data from at least 165 Snowflake customer accounts, according to Mandiant. Ticketmaster said about 560 million customers were affected. Santander US, Advance Auto Parts, and Pure Storage also disclosed incidents. Snowflake said it found no evidence of a vulnerability in its product.

The attackers used customer credentials stolen by infostealer malware, often from personal devices. Many accounts lacked MFA. That pattern should worry every cloud team. S3 bucket misconfigurations still cause leaks, but the fastest growing losses involve compromised identities, abused service principals, and excessive data exports.

## CSPM needs an identity sidecar

Cloud security posture management tools from Wiz, Prisma Cloud, Orca, and Microsoft Defender for Cloud remain useful. They find public storage, exposed admin ports, missing encryption, and dangerous network paths. But a valid user logging in from a new country and querying a billion-row table may look like normal API traffic to a posture scanner.

Cloud detection and response fills part of that gap. It connects AWS CloudTrail, Azure Activity, Google Cloud Audit Logs, Snowflake login history, Okta logs, and EDR telemetry. Detections should focus on new access from infostealer-linked IP addresses, mass table exports, changes to network policies, and user accounts that suddenly run admin commands.

## Data classification determines blast radius

Snowflake customers learned that warehouse security and data security are different problems. A single analyst account can access payment data, customer support records, and production backups if roles are built too broadly. Teams should map sensitive tables, tag them, enforce row-level or column-level security, and separate development, analytics, and production environments.

Vendor risk also matters. Customers must ask whether their SaaS provider enforces MFA, logs every administrative action, supports customer-managed keys, and notifies them of unusual queries. A SOC 2 report does not answer all of those questions.

## The practical 2025 cloud control plan

First, require MFA for every human account and use key rotation and workload identity for services. Second, export audit logs to a separate account that administrators cannot easily delete. Third, monitor bulk data exports and new OAuth clients. Fourth, test a forced credential reset and account isolation procedure.

The incident also exposed a staffing problem. Many cloud teams can configure storage but have not trained analysts to read data-warehouse logs. Snowflake query history, login history, and user-management events need correlation with endpoint telemetry. A sign-in from a personal device loaded with RedLine or Lumma should not look like a normal analytics session. Security teams should also test their ability to freeze access quickly. That means documented runbooks for revoking sessions, rotating passwords, disabling network policies, and contacting the vendor's security team. Waiting for an account manager during an active breach wastes hours. The strongest cloud programs put identity monitoring, data classification, and tested response together before the first unusual query hits a sensitive table.

The Snowflake campaign did not break the cloud. It exploited the predictable way companies connect people to data. In 2025, cloud security belongs to whoever can link a user, a device, a query, and a sensitive dataset in one alert.

## Provisioning is no longer the whole job

Okta's 2023 support-system breach exposed HTTP Archive files containing session tokens from customer interactions. The company repeatedly expanded its explanation as investigators found more evidence of access. The incident made one point clear: an identity provider is not merely an HR system for accounts. It is a security control plane, and its logs belong in incident response.

The same lesson appeared in the 2024 Snowflake campaign. Mandiant found that attackers logged in with stolen customer credentials and did not exploit a Snowflake product vulnerability. Once inside, they exported data before many customers noticed anything wrong.

## Standing privileges become exposed ports

IAM teams should start by counting standing privilege. That includes global administrators in Microsoft Entra ID, Okta super admins, AWS accounts with broad IAM rights, service principals with write access to production, and shared mailboxes used by finance teams. In 2025, those accounts deserve the same scrutiny as an internet-facing server.

Privileged access management products from CyberArk, BeyondTrust, Delinea, and Okta can enforce time-bound elevation. The target should be simple: no user keeps permanent admin rights unless a documented exception exists. Approval workflows should produce a ticket, an expiration time, and an audit record.

## Logs must trigger action

Entra ID sign-in logs, Okta System Logs, and cloud audit logs can detect common identity attacks: MFA fatigue, new trusted locations, token replay, suspicious OAuth grants, group membership changes, and reset of another user's password. Too many companies send these logs to a SIEM and never write detections.

Useful alerts include a new MFA method added shortly after a successful login, an admin account using a residential proxy, a service principal creating a new OAuth app, and mass changes to security groups. False positives will happen, but tuning is better than ignoring the data.

The most dangerous accounts are often not named after an administrator. A service account tied to a provisioning tool, a mailbox with delegation rights, or a developer account with permanent subscription access can be just as powerful. IAM teams should review those accounts and assign owners. They should also distinguish human users from workload identities. A CI/CD pipeline should use federated credentials or short-lived tokens, not a static access key stored in a wiki. Break-glass accounts remain necessary, but they should be excluded from normal policies, monitored closely, and used only during declared incidents. When access is centralized, one misconfigured policy can affect thousands of users. That concentration is a risk. It is also a chance to apply strong authentication, logging, and review consistently.

## Passkeys change the risk model

FIDO2 passkeys remove the password and block phishing relay attacks. Google reported passkey support for more than 400 million accounts in late 2023, but enterprise rollout remains uneven because of legacy devices, contractor access, and break-glass procedures.

A practical rollout starts with phishing-resistant authentication for admins and high-value users. It then adds passkeys to customer-facing or frontline workflows where SMS and push MFA create the most risk.

IAM cannot prevent every breach. But in 2025, it can detect the first unauthorized login, stop the second privileged action, and provide the logs that explain what happened. That is first-responder work.

## Finished reports miss the first 72 hours

Mandiant's M-Trends 2025 report said 54 percent of organizations were notified of a breach by an external party. That number is an intelligence failure. It means defenders often learn about incidents from Mandiant, Microsoft, a law enforcement notice, a ransomware leak site, or a business partner.

The gap is not a lack of indicators. Feeds can throw out millions of hashes and IP addresses every day. The gap is context. Which initial-access broker is selling VPN credentials in your sector? Which ransomware gang is recruiting corporate insiders? Which exploit just appeared in a Telegram channel before public scanning began?

Recorded Future, Flashpoint, Intel 471, KELA, and Unit 221B compete on access to forums, chat services, ransomware leak sites, and criminal marketplaces. That access can show a company's domain, VPN appliance, or employee credentials before a negotiation starts.

## Indicators need to become detections

Raw intelligence has little value unless it reaches EDR, SIEM, email security, and identity tools. A report mentioning Akira should become detections for renamed backup binaries, mass file extensions changes, and suspicious Group Policy updates. A warning about Citrix or Ivanti exploitation should trigger exposure checks and web-shell hunts.

CISA's Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog passed 1,200 entries in 2025. It is not a complete threat feed, but it is an excellent filter. If a CVE is in KEV, exposed to the internet, and tied to ransomware activity, patching should jump ahead of lower-risk work.

## Attribution still matters

Some executives treat attribution as academic. It is not. Attribution shapes insurer questions, legal strategy, sanctions referrals, and negotiation posture. Microsoft naming Storm-0501, Mandiant naming UNC5537, and CrowdStrike naming StellarParticle give defenders shared language. They also link tooling, targets, and infrastructure across incidents.

Threat teams should produce regular briefings for operations leaders, not just long PDFs. A useful briefing names the three groups most likely to hit the company, the techniques they use, the detections in place, and the controls still missing.

The biggest mistake is buying intelligence and leaving it in a portal. Analysts need a workflow for turning it into controls. If a report says a group exploits a particular firewall, asset management should identify every instance and networking should verify exposure. If a broker lists employee credentials, identity teams should force resets and check for recent MFA changes. If a ransomware gang targets healthcare or manufacturing, executives should know the likely business impact. Deception technology and internet-facing exposure management can add internal context. They show whether an attacker path actually reaches a crown-jewel system. Intelligence should also be measured in decision quality: did it change a patch priority, stop a vendor onboarding, or shorten an investigation? Those outcomes matter more than report count.

## The metric is action, not volume

A mature intelligence program tracks how many reports led to blocked access, patched systems, reset credentials, or changed coverage. It does not boast about how many IOCs it imported.

In 2025, ransomware gangs, state actors, and fraud rings operate in chat channels and private negotiations. Defenders who only consume public feeds will keep reading about themselves in someone else's report.

## Metadata can reveal enough

In April 2024, AT&T disclosed that 73 million current and former customer records had appeared on a criminal forum. The data did not include names or credit-card numbers in many records, but it contained phone numbers, call metadata, timestamps, and location-related routing information. Security researchers warned that such records can reveal relationships, routines, and sensitive contacts.

Weeks later, Ticketmaster confirmed a Snowflake-linked intrusion affecting about 560 million customers. The company said the data included names, addresses, emails, phone numbers, and ticket-order information, but generally not full payment-card numbers. That distinction mattered legally, but it did not make the data harmless.

## The 'no financial data' line is incomplete

Breach notices often emphasize what was not stolen: no Social Security numbers, no passwords, no full payment cards. That can be technically true while missing the real risk. Email addresses fuel phishing and credential stuffing. Phone numbers enable SIM swapping and smishing. Purchase history supports extortion and account takeover. Customer support notes can contain partial payment data, travel plans, or health information.

The SEC's 2023 cybersecurity disclosure rule requires public companies to disclose material incidents within four business days of determining materiality. State laws impose different notice timelines. Attorneys general in California, Texas, New York, and Massachusetts increasingly ask how a company scoped the affected data, when logging started, and whether third-party credentials were involved.

## Vendor breaches become customer crises

The Snowflake campaign exposed a recurring problem. A customer may not own the vulnerable system, but it owns the relationship with the people whose data was exposed. Ticketmaster users did not care whether the login came from an infostealer-infected personal device or a product flaw. They expected notice, credit protection where appropriate, and answers.

Security teams should map where regulated data travels: SaaS platforms, data warehouses, support tools, marketing systems, and analytics partners. Contracts should require breach notification timelines, audit logs, MFA, encryption, and indemnification. A SOC 2 report is a starting point, not a substitute for testing.

The Ticketmaster case also demonstrated how stolen data circulates. Threat actors advertised databases, journalists obtained samples, and customers learned details from public reporting before every affected person received notice. Companies should expect that timeline. A response plan should include a verified call center, credit monitoring when appropriate, clear FAQs, and a way to update affected individuals as investigation changes. Legal teams should not write notices in isolation. Engineers must validate claims about affected fields, support logs, and encryption. If a company says passwords were hashed, it should know the algorithm and whether any weak hashes were cracked. Vague notice language may reduce immediate calls, but it increases distrust when the next leak appears.

## Better analysis after the breach

After an incident, responders should produce a blast-radius report that lists data classes, affected populations, possible downstream abuse, logs used to scope the event, and evidence that access was revoked. The report should distinguish confirmed access from theoretical exposure. It should also say what was not seen, such as evidence of data exfiltration or administrator changes.

Breach notices in 2025 need more than reassurance. They need specificity. Customers, regulators, and boards can handle bad news. They have less patience for vague language months after the records disappeared.

## Fines are only the visible cost

In January 2025, the EU General Court largely upheld Ireland's 2023 decision against Meta over EU-to-US data transfers but reduced the fine from €1.2 billion to €110 million. The ruling kept the pressure on companies that rely on Standard Contractual Clauses without evaluating the actual legal risks of a transfer.

That case is GDPR's most famous example, but everyday compliance costs less dramatically. Teams spend money on access reviews, deletion workflows, vendor questionnaires, encryption, logging, and evidence collection. SOC 2 Type II audits add another layer, especially for B2B software companies whose customers demand proof before signing.

## Evidence beats policies

Auditors and regulators have grown tired of policies that nobody follows. A SOC 2 examiner wants to see termination tickets, change approvals, vulnerability scan results, access reviews, incident logs, and background-check records. A GDPR regulator wants to see how data minimization, lawful basis, retention, and subject-rights requests work in the product.

Companies should automate evidence collection wherever possible. Identity platforms can produce access-review exports. Jira or ServiceNow can show change approval. AWS, Azure, and GCP logs can support incident response and monitoring controls. Vanta, Drata, Secureframe, and OneTrust reduce manual collection, but they do not remove responsibility for fixing gaps.

## The scope keeps expanding

Financial firms faced DORA requirements beginning January 17, 2025. EU member states continued implementing NIS2 obligations across critical sectors. The SEC's four-day incident disclosure rule affects public companies. AI systems add new questions about training data, model access, logging, and customer data isolation.

A narrow SOC 2 report may no longer satisfy enterprise buyers. They ask about HIPAA, PCI DSS, ISO 27001, FedRAMP, regional data residency, subprocessor lists, and penetration tests. Security and legal teams should map controls once and reuse them across frameworks instead of running separate audits in silos.

The operational burden falls hardest on mid-sized companies. A startup closing an enterprise deal may receive hundreds of security questionnaires asking about encryption, incident response, subprocessor oversight, AI use, and deletion practices. Answering them manually wastes engineering time. A control library helps: write answers once, attach evidence, and update them after audits. Data mapping is equally important. Teams need to know where personal data enters the product, where it is stored, who can access it, and when it is deleted. Subject-access requests become painful when records are scattered across warehouses, support tools, and backup tapes. Compliance leaders should also monitor state privacy laws in California, Texas, Oregon, and Florida, because a single product may need multiple notice and deletion workflows.

## Liability does not disappear with a vendor

GDPR makes controllers responsible for how processors handle personal data. A SaaS vendor cannot simply absorb blame if it exposed customer records without MFA, weak logging, or poor subprocessor controls. Contracts must define notification timelines, audit rights, deletion requirements, and security baselines.

Compliance is getting more expensive because regulators and customers expect programs to operate continuously. The companies that handle SOC 2 and GDPR well in 2025 are not the ones with the thickest policy binders. They are the ones that can show an auditor evidence on demand and fix a failed control before it becomes a breach.

## Labels address the obvious failures

The White House and CISA launched the U.S. Cyber Trust Mark in 2024, with consumer labels expected to appear on more devices through 2025. The program builds on NIST criteria for IoT security: unique default credentials, disclosed update support, attack-surface reduction, secure data handling, and vulnerability disclosure.

The label cannot solve every IoT problem. It does, however, give buyers a reason to reject devices with hardcoded passwords, unencrypted update channels, or no way to report a flaw. For years, those basic failures powered botnets and gave attackers footholds in home, retail, hospital, and school networks.

## Old CVEs still power attacks

CISA's KEV catalog includes numerous IoT and network-device flaws. CVE-2023-1389, a command-injection issue in TP-Link Archer routers, was exploited by attackers including Mirai variants. D-Link, Netgear, Cisco RV-series, and Fortinet devices have also appeared in exploitation campaigns. The common pattern is predictable: an appliance exposed to the internet, weak credentials, and no easy update path.

Healthcare devices create additional risk. The FDA's premarket cybersecurity guidance now expects medical-device makers to identify risks, provide updates, and disclose how devices will be supported. Hospitals still run imaging systems, infusion pumps, and lab equipment that cannot be patched during clinical operations.

## Segmentation is the practical control

Organizations should not wait for a label before separating IoT devices from production systems. Cameras, printers, building controllers, sensors, and guest devices should live on dedicated VLANs with least-privilege access. Network access control can identify new devices, assign them to the right segment, and quarantine devices that fail posture checks.

DNS filtering, outbound traffic monitoring, and rate limiting can stop a compromised camera from joining a botnet or reaching a command server. Device inventory should record firmware versions, support windows, vendors, and owners. That sounds basic, but many teams still cannot list every IoT device on their network.

Manufacturers still ship devices with weak points. Some use phone-home services with hardcoded certificates. Others store credentials in mobile apps or rely on unauthenticated protocols. Buyers should require a software bill of materials for network-connected products and ask whether components such as BusyBox, OpenSSL, or embedded Linux kernels are supported. A $50 sensor can sit on a network for a decade, so total cost must include patching and replacement. Universities and school districts face a related challenge as IoT devices proliferate under separate budgets. Security teams should create a guest-like IoT network, require registration, and block peer-to-peer communication. The label may improve product design, but the enterprise still owns the network where insecure devices live.

## Buyers gain purchasing power

Procurement teams should ask vendors how long they will supply patches, whether updates are signed, whether a vulnerability disclosure policy exists, and how credentials are provisioned. If a vendor cannot answer, the device should not go on a sensitive network.

The Cyber Trust Mark is not a guarantee of safety. But in 2025, it gives security teams a market signal while segmentation, monitoring, and inventory remain the controls that actually stop IoT attacks from becoming enterprise incidents.

## A signed driver can still defeat protection

Endpoint detection and response changed ransomware defense, but attackers found a reliable workaround. They use legitimate but vulnerable signed drivers to terminate security processes, erase telemetry, or disable kernel callbacks. Bring-your-own-vulnerable-driver attacks have appeared in ransomware, espionage, and fraud campaigns.

CISA and vendors have flagged drivers such as Micro-Star International's RTCore64.sys, tracked as CVE-2019-16098, for abuse in the wild. The driver may have been shipped for hardware monitoring, but an attacker with administrative rights can use it to read and write kernel memory. The signature is valid. The function is dangerous.

## EDR moves deeper into the operating system

CrowdStrike, SentinelOne, Microsoft Defender for Endpoint, Palo Alto Cortex XDR, and BlackBerry now emphasize tamper protection, early-launch antimalware, Protected Process Light, and driver blocking. Microsoft's vulnerable driver blocklist prevents known bad drivers from loading on supported Windows systems. Windows 11 24H2 and Smart App Control increase the friction further.

These controls are not optional for high-risk endpoints. Domain controllers, admin workstations, hypervisors, and backup servers should have the strictest driver policy. If a business application requires an older driver, it should run on an isolated system with an exception review and documented owner.

## The server problem gets more attention

Laptops often receive EDR first, but servers are where ransomware actors want to go. They target file servers, hypervisors, SQL servers, and backup repositories. Patching servers is harder because of uptime requirements, but that is exactly why compensating controls matter: application allowlisting, restricted admin groups, network segmentation, and monitoring of driver loads.

Teams should monitor Event ID 6 for driver loads, Event ID 4697 for service installation, and EDR events for process termination or configuration changes. They should also block common living-off-the-land activity: renamed wbadmin, vssadmin, net stop WinDefend, and unexpected use of PsExec.

Ransomware actors also target the tools that administrators trust. They use remote monitoring and management software, virtualization platforms, and backup consoles because those products are designed to control many systems at once. That makes vendor hardening guides essential, not optional. Teams should restrict which accounts can log into RMM consoles, require MFA, alert on new agent deployments, and separate management traffic from employee VLANs. Server hardening should remove unused drivers and block unsigned kernel code where supported. Compatibility exceptions must come from engineering and expire after review. The endpoint agent is powerful enough to cause outages, as the July 2024 CrowdStrike Falcon incident proved, so organizations need staged rollouts, canary groups, and tested recovery media. Good endpoint protection in 2025 balances aggressive prevention with operational discipline.

## Endpoint is part of a chain

No EDR product stops every attack. The July 2024 CrowdStrike Falcon update outage affected about 8.5 million Windows devices and disrupted airlines and hospitals, showing that endpoint agents operate with deep system privilege. That makes change management, staged rollouts, and tested recovery procedures essential.

In 2025, endpoint protection is not just about detecting malware. It is about hardening the kernel, protecting the agent itself, and keeping servers from becoming the launch point for ransomware.

## A trusted update becomes the attack

In March 2023, attackers trojanized the 3CX desktop application for Windows and macOS. The signed update reached customers through normal software channels, and researchers linked the operation to North Korea-linked AppleJeus activity. Two years earlier, Kaseya VSA flaw CVE-2021-30116 let REvil push ransomware through managed service providers to roughly 1,500 downstream businesses.

Those events changed how enterprises think about suppliers. A vendor with good security can still be compromised through its development tools, build server, package repository, or signing process. The malicious code arrives with a familiar name and often a valid signature.

## Developer machines are production assets

Supply chain defense starts with the systems that build software. Build agents need patching, EDR, hardened access, and separate credentials from developer workstations. Administrators should restrict who can approve production builds, monitor changes to CI/CD pipelines, and alert on new secrets, modified build scripts, or unexpected package sources.

Open-source dependencies add another risk. Malicious packages in npm and PyPI commonly use typosquatting, dependency confusion, and stolen maintainer credentials. Teams should pin versions, use private repositories, review lockfiles, and apply scanners from Snyk, Socket, GitHub, or JFrog. A scanner alone will not stop a determined maintainer account compromise, but it catches many obvious attacks.

## Signing proves source only when the key is protected

Code signing tells customers that a file came from a holder of the certificate. It does not prove the file is safe if attackers stole the key or manipulated the build before signing. Companies should store signing keys in hardware security modules or managed key vaults, require approval for signing jobs, and log every use.

Software bills of materials help incident responders answer whether a product included a vulnerable library. SBOMs are less useful when they are generated once and never updated. They should be machine-readable, tied to build versions, and reviewed during procurement.

The software acquisition process also needs teeth. Procurement should not accept a vendor's claim that it follows secure development without evidence. For high-risk products, that evidence can mean a recent SOC 2 Type II report, a penetration-test letter, vulnerability disclosure policy, incident response history, and proof that production systems require MFA. For open-source components, teams should understand maintainer health. A package with one volunteer maintainer and thousands of downloads can be a weak link. Internal developers should review changes to build pipelines as carefully as application code. A one-line modification to a Dockerfile or CI variable can leak secrets or replace a binary. Supply chain security is tedious work, but the alternative is shipping an attacker's payload under your trusted signature.

## Customers still need telemetry

Even a trusted installer can spawn suspicious behavior: PowerShell downloads, new services, connections to unknown domains, or credential access. EDR and network monitoring remain essential because they see post-installation actions.

Enterprises should ask vendors for secure development attestations, penetration-test summaries, vulnerability disclosure timelines, and subprocessor lists. Critical vendors deserve more than a questionnaire. They deserve architecture reviews and incident-notification clauses.

The 2025 supply chain lesson is uncomfortable. Trust in a software update is not enough. Defenders must monitor the update process, the build system, and the behavior that follows installation.

## A default component became an emergency

On March 14, 2025, CISA added CVE-2025-1974 to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog and issued an emergency directive for federal civilian agencies. The flaw affected Kubernetes ingress-nginx, a widely used ingress controller. In certain configurations, an unauthenticated attacker could send a crafted request and achieve remote code execution.

Security vendors including Wiz, Prisma Cloud, and Akamai warned that vulnerable admission webhooks could be exposed to the internet. The exact number of vulnerable deployments was debated, but the operational point was clear: many teams did not know whether they ran ingress-nginx, who owned it, or whether it faced the public internet.

## KEV changes priorities

Vulnerability programs still drown in scanner output. Tenable, Qualys, and Rapid7 can find thousands of findings, but teams cannot patch everything at once. CISA's KEV catalog solves part of that problem by identifying vulnerabilities with evidence of exploitation. Under Binding Operational Directive 22-01, federal agencies must remediate listed flaws by the due date. Private companies increasingly use KEV as their own high-priority queue.

CVE-2025-1974 also highlighted why exposure matters. A critical CVE on an isolated test cluster is not the same risk as one on an internet-facing production cluster. EPSS scores can help estimate exploitation probability, but asset context determines urgency: internet exposure, data sensitivity, identity privileges, and compensating controls.

## Inventory is the missing control

The hardest question during IngressNightmare was not how to patch. It was where the software ran. Kubernetes clusters, virtual machines, edge appliances, and developer environments often fall outside traditional host inventory. A cluster may be managed by platform engineering, a line-of-business team, or a forgotten SaaS pilot.

Effective vulnerability management needs one owner for each asset, a service owner for each application, and a way to mark exceptions. When a new KEV appears, teams should be able to search for the affected version across cloud accounts, containers, images, code repositories, and third-party managed services. They should also know which systems have compensating controls, such as WAF rules or disabled admission webhooks.

Containers make ownership harder. A base image may be pulled from a public registry, customized by a product team, and deployed in a cloud account managed by platform operations. When a CVE arrives, no one wants to own the rebuild. Mature teams assign image owners, automate rebuilds, and maintain an inventory of running images. They also scan admission controllers and default add-ons, because those components have broad cluster rights. Cloud providers should apply platform patches, but customers remain responsible for configurations and third-party controllers. The lesson of IngressNightmare is that vulnerability management must cover software the team did not explicitly install. It may be a default chart, a managed add-on, or a developer test cluster. If it can reach production data, it needs an owner.

## Patching is a workflow, not a report

The best programs set SLAs by severity and exposure, route tickets automatically, and escalate missed deadlines. They verify remediation with rescans and runtime checks. They also retire unsupported software instead of carrying it as an accepted risk forever.

CVE-2025-1974 did not require exotic tradecraft. It required a common component, exposure, and a patch window. In 2025, that combination is still how too many breaches begin. The fix is not another scanner report. It is a process that finds the owner, applies the patch, and proves the risk is gone.

## The pitch shifted from chat to triage

Microsoft made Security Copilot generally available in April 2024, embedding generative AI across Sentinel, Defender, and Entra. CrowdStrike expanded Charlotte AI for alert triage and natural-language searches. Google Security AI and Palo Alto Networks Cortex XSIAM added similar assistant features. By mid-2025, the sales pitch had changed.

Buyers did not need another chat window. They needed fewer alerts, faster summaries, and help writing queries. IBM's 2024 Cost of a Data Breach report found that organizations extensively using AI and automation saved an average of $2.2 million compared with organizations that did not. That figure reflects efficiency, not magic.

## Analysts need explanations, not hallucinated certainty

AI assistants work best when they summarize known telemetry: related alerts, user context, MITRE ATT&CK techniques, recent patches, and similar incidents. A junior analyst can ask Microsoft Sentinel to generate a KQL query or ask CrowdStrike to explain why a process was flagged. The analyst still validates the result.

Vendors have added grounding to reduce fabrication. Assistants cite logs, show source events, and restrict actions through role-based access. Security leaders should test these products with real triage scenarios and measure time saved, false-positive reduction, and whether junior analysts make better decisions.

## Prompt injection targets the assistant

AI assistants create a new attack surface. If an assistant reads emails, web pages, tickets, or threat reports, attackers can hide instructions in that content. A malicious document might try to make the assistant exfiltrate data, disable a detection, or reveal its system prompt. Plugins that connect to Slack, ServiceNow, Microsoft Graph, or EDR tools increase the risk.

Controls matter. Enterprises should limit what data an assistant can read, require approval for write actions, avoid exposing secrets in prompts, and log every query and response. They should also treat AI-generated firewall rules or investigation steps like any other code: review before production.

Vendor claims deserve scrutiny. Some products label rule-based correlation as AI, while others send prompts to large language models without showing what data leaves the tenant. Security teams should ask where models are hosted, whether customer prompts are used for training, how long logs are retained, and which actions require human approval. Cost can also spiral if every analyst query invokes a premium model. Start with measurable use cases: summarize a phishing email, turn an incident timeline into a ticket, translate a firewall rule, or group duplicate alerts. Then compare the output against senior-analyst work. AI will not replace security judgment in 2025. Teams that use it well will let experienced analysts spend more time on hunting, containment, and threat modeling while machines handle the repetitive first pass.

## Deepfakes raise the cost of trust

The same technology that helps analysts also helps attackers. Voice-cloning vishing, AI-written phishing messages, and synthetic help-desk calls are becoming common. Abnormal Security, Proofpoint, Microsoft, and CrowdStrike have all reported more convincing business email compromise attempts.

The response is not to ban AI. It is to harden identity verification: callback procedures, phishing-resistant MFA, payment-approval workflows, and training that tells employees when a voice or video request may be synthetic.

In 2025, AI has a real place in security operations. The successful deployments will be the ones that keep humans responsible, ground answers in evidence, and use automation to cut through alert noise instead of adding more.

Adaptive ANC now uses a microphone array that samples ambient sound 40,000 times per second. On the New York City subway, the XM6 erased roughly 80 percent of the low-frequency rumble. If you own the XM5, skip it. If you are coming from older buds or a competitor, the XM6 is among the best-sounding, best-canceling pairs you can buy right now — just keep the case in a consistent spot.

## A familiar design with a new trick on the wrist

The Apple Watch Series 11 looks identical to the Series 10. Same rounded edges, same 42mm and 46mm size options, same OLED display. The aluminum model starts at $399; the stainless steel version jumps to $699. If you were expecting a visual overhaul, look elsewhere.

What changed is inside. The new S11 SiP is roughly 20 percent faster, though in everyday use — checking notifications, starting a workout, using Apple Pay — the difference between S10 and S11 is unnoticeable. The display now peaks at 3,000 nits outdoors, up from 2,000. On a bright San Francisco afternoon, I could read a text without cupping my hand over the screen. That is a bigger deal than it sounds, especially if you run or cycle outdoors and need to glance at pace data at a glance.

## Hypertension awareness arrives

The headline feature is the hypertension detection system. It is not a medical-grade blood pressure cuff. Instead, the watch uses optical sensors and algorithms to flag trends that may indicate elevated blood pressure over time. After the required 14-day calibration period with a traditional cuff, the watch started providing weekly trend reports.

I compared its readings against a validated Omron cuff over three weeks. The watch consistently trended 5 to 8 mmHg low on systolic readings, but the directional accuracy — whether my pressure was rising or falling week over week —was reliable. Apple is transparent about the feature's limitations, and the FDA clearance is for awareness, not diagnosis. Treat it as a nudge to see a doctor, not a replacement for a real reading. The watch can also store a history of readings in the Health app, which is useful data to bring to a physician visit.

## The sleep coaching surprise

The unsung improvement is the updated sleep tracking. watchOS 12 combines heart rate variability, respiratory rate, wrist temperature, and movement into a single "Sleep Readiness" score each morning. After a week of late deadlines and early flights, the score correctly identified that I was running on fumes and suggested a rest day from workouts. The sleep staging (light, deep, REM) tracks closely with Garmin and Whoop data I have used, and the watch now tracks respiratory rate more accurately than the Series 10.

The Double Tap gesture returns from the Series 9, and Apple added a new pinch-and-hold command that triggers Siri without saying anything. It works reliably one-handed while holding coffee or a dog leash, though it occasionally triggers when adjusting the band. Charging speeds remain unchanged: zero to 80 percent in about 45 minutes on the included magnetic puck.

Battery life remains at 18 hours, which means you still charge it every night. The low-power mode extends that to about 36 hours, but it disables always-on display and background heart-rate measurements. For $399, the Series 11 is a modest update. But if you use an Apple Watch primarily for health and sleep insights, the hypertension awareness feature and improved sleep coaching make it worth the jump from a Series 8 or older.

## The weight loophole gets a serious upgrade

The 249-gram weight class matters because, in the United States, drones under 250 grams do not require registration for recreational use. The DJI Mini 4 Pro was already a capable flyer; the Mini 5 Pro tightens every screw.

The camera now uses a 1/1.3-inch sensor with an f/1.7 aperture, up from the 1/1.3-inch f/1.7 in the Mini 4 Pro — same sensor size, but the new lens is sharper at the edges and has less distortion. It shoots 4K at up to 120 frames per second, and the HDR pipeline handles high-contrast skies without the banding that plagued earlier Mini models. I flew it over the Pacific coast at golden hour and the footage held detail in both the bright water and the dark cliffside without requiring ND filters. The new Night Mode pulls usable video in conditions where the Mini 4 Pro produced a noisy mess.

## Flying it feels almost unfair

Omnidirectional obstacle sensing means the Mini 5 Pro sees in all directions, not just forward and backward. I deliberately flew it toward a tree at speed and it stopped, rerouted, and continued on its way. The Advanced Pilot Assistance Systems 4.0 (APAS) is genuinely impressive — it weaves around obstacles rather than just freezing. The ActiveTrack 360 subject tracking follows cars, boats, and people with smooth results. I tracked a cyclist along a coastal road and the drone kept the subject framed while navigating around streetlights and a low bridge.

Battery life is rated at 34 minutes per Intelligent Flight Battery. In real-world flying, with wind and sport mode bursts, I got 28 to 30 minutes. The new O4 video transmission system has a range of up to 20 kilometers, though line-of-sight rules mean you will rarely push that far. The Mini 5 Pro handles wind better than its predecessor. On a bluff with sustained 18 mph gusts, it held position without the alarming drift I saw on the Mini 4 Pro. DJI rates it for Level 5 wind resistance, up to 24 mph. The new Cruise Control feature locks in a forward speed with one button press, useful for smooth tracking shots without holding the stick. Return-to-home worked flawlessly even when I flew behind a small hill that briefly blocked the signal.

The RC 2 controller ($249 if bought separately) has a bright built-in screen, so you do not need to use your phone.

## The price keeps climbing

The standard Mini 5 Pro with the RC-N3 controller starts at $759. The Fly More Combo, which includes three batteries, a charging hub, and a shoulder bag, costs $1,039. That is $60 more than the Mini 4 Pro launched at. For a drone in this weight class, it is expensive.

The lack of a 1-inch sensor still separates it from the Air 3S, which costs $1,099 and has a larger sensor and dual-camera system. But the Air 3S weighs 249 grams more and requires FAA registration. For travel photographers and casual pilots, the tradeoff favors the Mini 5 Pro. If you already own a Mini 4 Pro, the improvements are incremental enough to wait for a sale.

## The floor is no longer aspirational

Three years ago, a robot vacuum under $350 meant a bumping disk that got lost under the couch and forgot where the dock was. That is no longer true. The Roborock Q Revo Lite and the Ecovacs Deebot T30 Pro both use LiDAR navigation, both mop and vacuum, and both self-empty their dustbins — features that used to cost twice as much.

I set both loose in my 900-square-foot apartment for three weeks. The Q Revo Lite mapped the space in its first run, dividing it into rooms with reasonable accuracy. I had to nudge a couple of boundaries in the app — it thought my kitchen island was a separate room — but after that, it cleaned on schedule without incident. The 5,500 Pa suction picked up cat litter, breakfast cereal, and the mysterious crumbs that accumulate under a toddler's high chair. On low-pile carpet, the boost mode increased suction automatically and the difference in deep-cleaning was visible when I emptied the bin.

## Mopping is the surprise

Both robots mop. The Q Revo Lite uses a spinning mop pad system that lifts 12 mm when it detects carpet, which means you do not have to swap attachments between hard floors and rugs. The Deebot T30 Pro uses a similar lift system but also has a hot-air mop-drying feature in the dock, which prevents the mildew smell that develops when a wet pad sits for days.

After a pasta sauce splatter incident, I ran both robots over the dried mess with no pre-treatment. The Q Revo Lite smeared it around on the first pass but got it on the second. The T30 Pro's oscillating mop was more aggressive and cleaned it in one go. Neither replaces a hands-on scrub for truly stuck-on food, but for daily maintenance, both are good enough that I stopped hand-mopping entirely. The self-emptying docks hold about 60 days of debris before the bag needs replacing, and the Q Revo Lite's dock also washes and dries the mop pads with hot air.

## What you give up at this price

The Q Revo Lite's app has ads for Roborock accessories, which is annoying. The T30 Pro has a shorter 150-minute runtime compared with the Q Revo Lite's 200 minutes. Neither has AI obstacle recognition — they will plow through a loose charging cable if you leave one on the floor. The T30 Pro's LiDAR turret is taller, which means it cannot fit under my low-clearance couch, while the Q Revo Lite cleared it easily.

Both robots register around 60 to 65 decibels on carpet during a standard clean — quieter than a conversation but audible from the next room. The Q Revo Lite runs slightly louder due to its stronger suction motor, while the T30 Pro is a touch quieter on hard floors. Replacement side brushes cost $12 for a two-pack, and mop pads run $18 a pair, reasonable compared to flagship accessory pricing.

At $299 and $279 respectively, these are not premium robots. But they are good enough that the value gap between a budget bot and a $1,000 flagship has narrowed considerably. If you have been waiting to pull the trigger, this is the year budget robot vacuums stopped feeling like a compromise.

## The rabbit hole starts with one switch

I have typed on membrane keyboards, chiclet keyboards, and the occasional office mechanical. I never understood the hobby. Then I spent an afternoon building a Keychron Q1 Pro with Gateron Brown tactile switches, PBT double-shot keycaps, and a screw-in stabilizer kit. The total came to $178 with the keycaps. Pre-built mechanical keyboards from the same manufacturer cost about $20 less.

The process took two hours. I watched three YouTube tutorials, bent one switch pin (easily straightened with a small screwdriver), and forgot to lube the stabilizers on the first pass. The result was a keyboard that sounds and feels unlike anything I have used. The Brown switches have a gentle bump on each keystroke without the loud click of Cherry MX Blues. Typing this review on it, I am more aware of each press, but not in a distracting way. My typing accuracy improved because the tactility gives clear feedback that a key has registered.

## The Q1 Pro is a serious piece of kit

The Q1 Pro has a full aluminum case, a gasket-mount design, and supports both Bluetooth 5.1 and wired USB-C. It connects to my MacBook, my work laptop, and my iPad, switching between them with a function-key command. South-facing RGB LEDs glow through the keycaps, and the QMK/VIA firmware means every key is remappable without installing sketchy software. I remapped Caps Lock to Escape and put the Delete key where Backspace usually lives, which sounds minor but makes a measurable difference for someone who writes all day.

I averaged three weeks between charges with light daily use and the LEDs switched off. This may sound ridiculous if you have never paid attention to keyboard acoustics, but once you hear the difference, a $20 membrane board feels like typing on a cafeteria tray. The screw-in stabilizers, after I properly lubed them with dielectric grease, eliminated the rattle on the spacebar and larger keys that plagues stock boards.

If you type for a living and spend eight hours a day at a keyboard, yes.
