## Fitness tracking that means something

Garmin's Firstbeat analytics engine is a generation ahead of Apple's workout app. The Venu 3 tracks running dynamics (ground contact time, vertical oscillation, stride length), estimated training load, VO2 max, and recovery time. After a hard interval session, the watch told me to take 46 hours off before my next hard effort. I ignored it once, ran too soon, and felt heavy for three days. The race predictor feature estimated my 5K time within 10 seconds of my actual PR, which is better accuracy than I expected from a wrist sensor.

The sleep coach is excellent. It combines HRV, respiratory rate, blood oxygen, and movement into a simple score with actionable advice. The Venu 3 also stores up to 650 songs offline for phone-free runs, and I synced a Spotify playlist in about four minutes over Wi-Fi.

The body battery feature — Garmin's energy reserve metric — is a surprisingly useful proxy for when to push through an afternoon slump versus when to call it. On mornings after poor sleep, the body battery started low and the watch suggested a recovery walk instead of a run.

## What you give up

The Venu 3 is not a smartwatch in the Apple sense. Notifications are basic. You can read a text but you cannot reply from the watch (unless you use an Android phone with canned responses). There is no App Store, no Apple Pay alternative with the same merchant coverage, and the touchscreen is less responsive than an Apple Watch. Garmin Pay works at fewer terminals. I missed being able to pay for coffee with my wrist during the first week, but I adapted by carrying a card.

The AMOLED display is sharp and bright, but the always-on mode reduces battery life to about six days. The watch is also thicker and heavier (47 grams) than the Series 11. If your priority is fitness and endurance, the Venu 3 is the best GPS watch in its price range. If you want a wrist computer that handles messages, payments, and apps, stick with Apple.

## A wearable display, not a holographic computer

The XREAL Air 2 Ultra looks like a chunky pair of sunglasses. At 80 grams, it is light enough to wear for a couple of hours, and the electrochromic lenses can switch between transparent and opaque with a button on the temple. There is no onboard processor, no battery in the frames — it is a display that tethers to a phone, PC, or the XREAL Beam Pro accessory ($139).

That tether is both the limitation and the point. The dual Sony Micro-OLED panels deliver 1,920 x 1,080 per eye at 120 Hz, creating a virtual screen that XREAL says is equivalent to a 52-inch display viewed from 15 feet away. On a flight from Seattle to Tokyo, I watched three movies on the Air 2 Ultra connected to my MacBook. The experience was closer to a private theater than a phone screen. The image is sharp in the center, though text at the edges softens slightly, and the field of view is 52 degrees — enough for immersion but not as enveloping as the Apple Vision Pro's 100-plus degrees.

## 6DoF and hand tracking are a work in progress

The Ultra model adds two cameras on the bridge for six-degree-of-freedom tracking and hand gesture recognition. In the Nebula software environment, you can open multiple virtual screens — a browser, a Slack window, a YouTube video — and position them around a virtual room. I set up three screens on my desk and used them for an afternoon. The concept is compelling. The execution is rough.

Hand tracking lost my fingers whenever I moved quickly, and typing on a virtual keyboard with midair taps is slow enough to be a novelty. The virtual monitors are lower resolution than a physical display — roughly 720p equivalent per window — which makes text-heavy work tiring after 30 minutes. The Beam Pro accessory improves the experience by adding spatial computing features without draining your phone's battery, but at $139 on top of the $699 glasses, the total investment approaches the cost of a used Meta Quest 3.

## The $699 question

If you want a private, immersive display for media consumption on planes or in hotel rooms, the standard XREAL Air 2 at $399 is the better value. The Ultra exists for developers and early adopters who want to experiment with spatial computing without dropping $3,499 on an Apple Vision Pro.

The Air 2 Ultra is not the future of AR that Meta's Orion prototype promises. There are no holographic overlays on the real world, no AI assistant identifying objects in your field of view. What it is, today, is a wearable monitor that works. The electrochromic dimming is genuinely useful, and the build quality is solid for a first-generation product. But the software needs another year of polish, and the tethered design means you always need a companion device. That might be enough to justify the price — but only if you travel constantly and hate your laptop screen.

## A power bank that tells you what it is doing

The Anker 737 Power Bank (PowerCore 24K) is a 24,000 mAh brick with a small monochrome display on the front. The screen shows input wattage, output wattage per port, remaining battery percentage, and estimated time to full recharge. That last detail sounds trivial until you are sitting at an airport gate trying to decide whether you have 20 minutes to top up before boarding.

It has two USB-C ports and one USB-A port. The first USB-C port delivers up to 140W output, enough to charge a 16-inch MacBook Pro at full speed. The second USB-C port outputs up to 100W, and the USB-A port handles 22.5W. Total output is 160W across all ports. During a conference week, I charged my MacBook Pro, iPhone, and AirPods Pro simultaneously from the 737 while it itself was plugged into a wall outlet — passthrough charging works without issue, and the power bank prioritizes charging connected devices before refilling its own battery.

## Real-world capacity

At 24,000 mAh at 3.2V, the 737 is rated at 86.4 watt-hours, which is below the 100 Wh FAA limit for carry-on luggage. I had no trouble going through airport security, and the gate agent at a small regional airport did not give it a second glance.

In testing, the 737 charged my iPhone 15 Pro from 0 to 100 percent roughly four times before needing a recharge itself. It charged a 14-inch MacBook Pro (M3 Pro) from 20 percent to 80 percent in about 50 minutes while the laptop was in use. The 140W output makes a noticeable difference compared with 65W or 100W batteries when you are working and charging simultaneously — the MacBook did not throttle under load. For a Nintendo Switch, the 737 provided about three full charges. For a camera battery charger, it kept my Sony a7 IV topped up through a full day of shooting.

## The weight problem

This thing weighs 630 grams, or 1.39 pounds. It is not a pocket power bank. It lives in a backpack or a briefcase. The chassis is made of matte polycarbonate that feels durable but picks up scuffs. The display is useful but adds a small parasitic drain — Anker says the idle draw is minimal, and over a week of sitting in my bag, the battery dropped from 100 to 93 percent. The power bank supports trickle-charging mode for low-power devices like Bluetooth earbuds and smartwatches, which prevents the battery from shutting off when it detects a small load.

At $109.99, the 737 is not cheap. The Anker 535 (20,000 mAh, 65W) costs $59 but cannot charge a laptop at full speed. If you travel with a laptop and need a single brick that can keep every device alive across a long travel day, there is nothing else at this price that delivers 140W output with this kind of capacity. It is boring, heavy, and I will not leave home without it — even on day trips where I doubt I will need the extra juice.

## The cable label you need to read

Walk into any electronics store and you will see a bin of USB-C cables priced from $5 to $35. They all fit the same port. They do not all do the same job.

A USB-C cable has two independent capabilities: power delivery and data transfer. A cable that charges your phone at 20W may not carry a video signal to a monitor. A cable that supports Thunderbolt 4 data at 40 Gbps may only deliver 100W of power. The only way to know is to read the fine print on the packaging or look for logos. The USB-IF certifies cables, and certified ones carry a logo that indicates their speed and wattage. If a cable has no logo, assume it is USB 2.0 data (480 Mbps) and charging-only.

For charging, the spec that matters is the wattage rating. A 60W cable handles most laptops. A 100W or 240W cable is needed for 16-inch MacBook Pros or gaming laptops that draw more power. For data, USB 3.2 Gen 2 supports 10 Gbps. USB4 and Thunderbolt 4 support 40 Gbps, which is what you need for external SSDs or external displays at 4K/60Hz. The new USB4 v2 spec supports 80 Gbps, but cables are still rare and expensive.

## Three cables I use every day

The Anker 515 USB-C to USB-C cable (6 feet, 100W, USB 3.1 Gen 2) is my daily workhorse. It charges a MacBook Pro, transfers data to external SSDs, and costs $15.99. The braided nylon has held up for over a year without fraying. I keep one at my desk and one in my bag.

For travel, I carry the Cable Matters 240W USB-C cable (3.3 feet). It is shorter but rated for 240W and USB4 at 40 Gbps. It handles everything from charging a Razer Blade 18 to connecting a CalDigit TS4 dock. At $19.99, it is the single cable I grab when I want to travel light. The short length is actually a benefit on the road — no cable spaghetti in the hotel room.

For the bedside table, the Apple USB-C Charge Cable (1 meter, 60W) is the one that came with my MacBook. It is only USB 2.0 data speeds (480 Mbps), but for overnight charging, that does not matter. If you are buying a third-party cable for data transfer, avoid the ones that do not list a data speed — they are often USB 2.0 only.

## The e-waste angle

The European Union's USB-C mandate went into full effect in December 2024, and every phone sold in the EU now uses the port. Apple's transition to USB-C with the iPhone 15 line means the Lightning cable is effectively legacy. But the average household still has a drawer of cables that do not clearly indicate their capabilities.

The simplest rule: if the cable is thicker and less flexible, it usually carries more power and data. If it came free with a phone and is thin as a noodle, assume it is charge-only. Label the good ones with a small piece of tape. Keep three. Donate or recycle the rest. Your future self will thank you at 30,000 feet when the one cable you packed actually works.

## The tablet itself is excellent

The 13-inch M4 iPad Pro weighs 1.28 pounds and is 5.1 mm thin. The new M4 chip has a 10-core CPU and a 10-core GPU, and it scored 2,850 in Geekbench 6 single-core and 11,200 in multi-core — numbers that rival a 15-inch MacBook Air with the M3. The Tandem OLED display is the best screen Apple has ever put on a portable device: 1,000 nits full-screen brightness, 1,600 nits peak HDR, and perfect blacks.

For media consumption, drawing with the Apple Pencil Pro, and tablet-native apps like Procreate and LumaFusion, the M4 iPad Pro has no peer. The Pencil Pro's new squeeze and barrel-roll features work well in supported apps, and the hover precision is sharp enough for detailed illustration. Procreate on the M4 runs brushes and layers that would stutter on an M2 iPad, and LumaFusion exports a 4K timeline faster than my MacBook Air M2. The four-speaker audio system is loud enough to fill a hotel room without distortion.

## The keyboard calculus

The Magic Keyboard for the 13-inch iPad Pro costs $349 and adds 1.5 pounds, bringing the total to 2.78 pounds — more than a 13-inch MacBook Air M3 (2.7 pounds), which starts at $1,099. An iPad Pro 13-inch with Magic Keyboard and Pencil Pro costs $1,647 before storage upgrades. The 256GB base model is $1,299; 1TB adds $400.

The keyboard itself is good. The function row is backlit, the trackpad is glass and supports all the multi-touch gestures, and the aluminum palm rest feels premium. But iPadOS still treats external displays as an afterthought. Stage Manager on iPad is better than it was two years ago, but it is still a cramped window-management system that fights you when you try to work with more than three apps simultaneously. Using the iPad Pro as a primary work machine can make frequent switching between a Google Doc, a Slack window, and a browser with multiple tabs feel cumbersome.

## When the iPad Pro wins

The M4 iPad Pro makes sense for three groups. Digital artists and illustrators who use Procreate benefit from the Pencil Pro and the OLED display in ways a Mac cannot match. Students who take handwritten notes with the Apple Pencil will appreciate the tablet form factor and long battery life (16 hours in our video-loop test). And people who already own a Mac but want a secondary device for media, reading, and light work will find the iPad Pro a compelling companion.

It does not make sense as a laptop replacement for someone who needs multiple windows, external storage, and a desktop-class browser. iPadOS 18 improved multitasking, but it is still not macOS. At $1,299 for the base model, the M4 iPad Pro is a brilliant tablet that asks you to accept its limitations. The Magic Keyboard is a $349 reminder that Apple still has not decided what this device wants to be when it grows up.

## The screen was worth the wait

The original Steam Deck LCD had a 7-inch, 800p, 60Hz display that was functional but washed out. The Steam Deck OLED upgrades to a 7.4-inch, 1,280 x 800 HDR OLED panel with a 90Hz refresh rate. The difference is not subtle. Black levels are true, colors are vibrant without being oversaturated, and the 90Hz option makes desktop navigation and supported games like Hollow Knight: Silksong feel noticeably smoother. The display also reaches 1,000 nits of peak brightness, which makes the Deck usable outdoors on a shaded patio — the LCD model was essentially an indoor-only device.

The APU is still the same custom AMD Aerith chip (Zen 2 CPU, RDNA 2 GPU), but the memory is faster: 16GB of LPDDR5X at 6,400 MT/s instead of 5,500. The bump is modest in benchmark terms but reduces stuttering in memory-heavy games like Baldur's Gate 3. The 6nm refresh of the APU is also more efficient, which contributes to the improved battery life.

## Battery life and thermals

Valve rates the Steam Deck OLED at 3 to 12 hours depending on the game. Actual battery life varies considerably by game, display brightness, resolution, graphics settings, and performance limits.. More demanding games can reduce battery life substantially and 40 minutes. Indie 2D games consistently pushed past 6 hours, which makes the Deck a genuine travel companion for flights and hotel rooms.

The fan is quieter. The LCD Deck had a high-pitched whine that kicked in during demanding games; the OLED model produces a lower, less intrusive whoosh. It is still audible in a quiet room, but it no longer sounds like a small vacuum. The redesigned heat pipe and larger exhaust vent help, and the back panel stays cooler during long sessions.

## The competition is real

The ASUS ROG Ally X ($799) uses a faster AMD Z1 Extreme chip and a 1080p VRR display. It outperforms the Steam Deck in raw framerates but runs Windows, which means you deal with driver updates, background processes, and a less controller-friendly interface. The Lenovo Legion Go S ($499) runs SteamOS but uses the lower-powered Z1 Go chip and has a smaller 7-inch screen. The Ayaneo Pocket S ($799) is smaller and more powerful but has software bugs and worse build quality.

At $549 for the 512GB OLED model, the Steam Deck OLED still hits the best balance of price, performance, and software. SteamOS suspends and resumes instantly. Sleep mode works the way a handheld should — press the power button, put it down, come back three days later, and your game is exactly where you left it. Windows handhelds still struggle with that. The software library is the full Steam catalog, and Proton compatibility has improved to the point where most games run without tinkering.

If you already own a Steam Deck LCD, the OLED upgrade is worth it only if you play primarily in handheld mode and care about the screen. If you have been waiting for the right time to buy a gaming handheld, this is it. Valve set the bar, and the competition is still catching up.

## A thermostat that knows which room you are in

The 4th-generation Nest Learning Thermostat costs $279 and comes with one Nest Temperature Sensor in the box. The previous generation required you to buy sensors separately for $39 each, and they were unreliable — they dropped off the network and their readings lagged by 15 minutes or more.

The new sensor uses Thread networking instead of Wi-Fi, which means it connects through a Thread border router (like a Nest Hub or Apple TV 4K) rather than directly to your Wi-Fi. The result is faster response times and better reliability. I placed a sensor in my bedroom, and the thermostat now uses that reading at night instead of the hallway sensor near the front door, which always ran 3 degrees colder. Within two nights, the bedroom stayed at a consistent 68 degrees instead of swinging between 65 and 72. Adding a second sensor to my home office was a five-minute process in the Google Home app.

## The display and interface got a refresh

The thermostat itself has a brighter, higher-contrast display and a new mirrored finish that looks less like plastic and more like glass. The interface still uses the familiar rotating ring, but Google added a few new screens: a live energy usage dashboard, a humidity trend graph, and a "comfort profile" that learns how long your HVAC system takes to reach a target temperature. If your house takes 20 minutes to cool from 75 to 70, the Nest starts the AC 20 minutes before your scheduled setpoint rather than at the scheduled time.

The learning algorithm has improved. The previous Nest would detect when I was away by using motion sensing on the thermostat itself, which meant it could not tell if someone was in a back bedroom. The 4th-gen model uses the temperature sensors and their built-in motion detectors to determine occupancy across multiple rooms. During my test week, it correctly identified that I was working from the home office on a Tuesday and did not switch to Eco mode. On Thursday, when I left for a day trip, it detected the empty house within 30 minutes and set back the temperature.

## Matter and energy savings

Matter support means the thermostat works with Apple Home, Google Home, Amazon Alexa, and Samsung SmartThings without needing separate integrations. I set it up in Apple Home and it appeared within seconds. Siri can change the temperature, and the thermostat responds to automations from any platform. The C-wire requirement remains — if your old thermostat does not have a common wire, Google includes a C-wire adapter in the box, but installation is more involved.

Google claims the Nest saves an average of 10 to 12 percent on heating and 15 percent on cooling. My July electric bill was $18 lower than the same month last year, though some of that is due to milder weather. The energy dashboard shows runtime history and suggests temperature setbacks based on your schedule, and the Seasonal Savings feature automatically makes small adjustments over time.

At $279, the 4th-gen Nest is $30 more than the 3rd-generation model it replaces. The included sensor and improved reliability make it worth the upgrade if you are coming from an older Nest or a dumb thermostat. If you already have a 3rd-gen Nest with working sensors, wait until they fail.

## A speaker that knows what it is

The Bose SoundLink Max weighs 2.8 pounds, measures 9.4 x 4.1 x 3.2 inches, and comes in black or blue finish. It has a woven steel mesh grille, a silicone rubber body, and a fabric carry loop on one end. It looks like a serious portable speaker rather than a fashion accessory. The controls — power, Bluetooth, volume, and a multifunction button — are physical and easy to find by touch, which matters when you are cooking or packing a cooler.

For $199, it competes directly with the JBL Xtreme 4 ($249), the Sony SRS-XG300 ($199), and the UE Hyperboom ($329). The category is crowded, but Bose's approach is different: this speaker is tuned for vocal clarity and midrange warmth rather than maximum bass output. The SoundLink Max uses a custom transducer and a passive radiator, and Bose's digital signal processing keeps the sound balanced at any volume.

## How it sounds

The SoundLink Max is positioned as a larger, more powerful portable speaker than compact models such as the JBL Charge 5, while competing with products such as the Sonos Move 2. On acoustic tracks —Nick Drake's "Pink Moon," Big Thief's "Spud Infinity" —the Bose was the clear winner. Guitar strings had texture, Adrianne Lenker's voice sat forward in the mix, and the soundstage felt wider than the speaker's size suggested. The Charge 5 sounded muddy by comparison, with vocals buried under boosted low end.

On electronic and hip-hop — Kendrick Lamar's "Not Like Us," Fred again..'s "Delilah (pull me out of this)" —the SoundLink Max held its own but did not rattle the windows the way the JBL Xtreme 4 does. Bass is present and controlled, with a low-end extension that surprised me given the speaker's compact size, but it is not boosted. If you want chest-thumping low end for a backyard party, the Xtreme 4 is the better pick. If you want a speaker that sounds good across genres without you needing to adjust the EQ, the Bose is more refined.

At higher volumes, the SoundLink Max stays composed. There is no distortion at 80 percent volume, and the stereo imaging remains stable even when you walk around the room. The speaker uses Bose's proprietary PositionIQ technology, which detects whether the speaker is upright or on its back and adjusts the EQ accordingly. I set it on its side in a cupholder at a park picnic and the sound did not suffer.

## Battery and connectivity

Bose rates the SoundLink Max at 20 hours at moderate volume. At full volume, I got just under 9 hours. Charging is via USB-C, and a full charge takes about 3 hours. There is no wireless charging and no built-in microphone for speakerphone calls, both of which are omissions at this price. The IP67 rating means it survives dust, dirt, and full submersion in up to a meter of water for 30 minutes — I hosed it off after a beach day without issue.

Bluetooth 5.3 supports multipoint connection, so you can pair two devices simultaneously and switch between them. The range is rated at 30 feet; I maintained a connection through two interior walls at about 40 feet. There is no Wi-Fi, no AirPlay, and no voice assistant — this is a pure Bluetooth speaker. If you want multi-room audio or AirPlay 2, you need a Sonos. If you want a rugged, great-sounding portable speaker that you can toss in a bag and bring to a picnic, the SoundLink Max is one of the best in its price range.
